doc_summary: Carlini gives an opinionated guide to doing high-impact research: choose problems by taste and impact, de-risk early, kill weak projects, execute experiments with unreasonable rigor, and write for a specific skeptical reader. Little of it addresses eval realism directly, but it shows how he picks what to test and what he counts as convincing evidence.

items.claim: prefers anticipating and pre-empting skeptical objections with extra controls over leaving results as suggestive, because convincing evidence means a skeptic has no obvious unanswered question about the setup.
items.quote: Every experiment should be as precisely performed as you can manage. Run multiple trials. Control for confounders. If there's a question a skeptical reader might ask about your setup, run the experiment that answers it before they ask.

items.claim: prefers evidence so overwhelming that the reader reaches the conclusion themselves over stating a claim outright, because a reader who thinks 'not me' is lost before the evidence lands.
items.quote: if I'd just said it outright in the intro, the reader's immediate reaction would have been "well, not me," and I'd have lost them before I started. So the job of the paper was to provide evidence so overwhelming that by the end, the reader arrives at that conclusion on their own.

items.claim: Starts with the sub-problem most likely to fail and uses small prototypes rather than polished experiments, so that doubts about the core idea are resolved cheaply and early.
items.quote: The best way I've found to minimize wasted time is to start with the sub-problem most likely to fail. It's comforting to work on the parts of a problem you know how to solve, but this teaches you nothing about whether your idea is any good.

items.claim: Distrusts field-standard methodology and evaluation conventions that were adopted without justification, because early arbitrary choices or famous-but-wrong papers get propagated uncritically.
items.quote: These are directions where someone (usually someone famous!) published an influential paper that got something critical wrong with the approach, methodology, or evaluation... and then the rest of the field followed along the same wrong direction without thinking critically about the initial choice

items.claim: prefers re-deriving a simpler, principled formulation (e.g. membership inference as a hypothesis test with a different metric) over inheriting convoluted existing evaluation setups, because the field's conventions can be confused and overcomplicated.
items.quote: The paper I eventually wrote argued the field should use a much simpler approach---treating membership inference as the hypothesis test it actually is---and evaluate using a different metric. A few years on, that's what everyone does.

items.claim: Chooses what to test by looking for areas where current practice looks obviously wrong and things that will matter soon, rather than topics that are merely tractable.
items.quote: How do you know when you have something only you can do? I look for areas where, when I read the work, I want to scream. Areas where you keep asking yourself "why is everyone doing this obviously wrong?"

items.claim: Tests whether a project is worth pursuing by writing the best-case conclusion before running experiments, and abandons it if the success case offers no insight beyond the numbers.
items.quote: I ask: if this paper were to succeed wildly---if all the experiments turned out exactly as I want---what could I say in a conclusion? If I have nothing to say beyond repeating the results, then what I've done mustn't have mattered very much.

items.claim: prefers strengthening a vague 'sometimes' into a quantified 'usually' over reporting a loose demonstration, because careful, precise execution is what makes a finding credible.
items.quote: On multiple occasions I've put in several hours of work just to strengthen a "sometimes" to "usually", because this is what it means to care.

items.claim: Anchors claims in real, concrete attack demonstrations (e.g. buying expired domains in LAION-5b) rather than hypothetical threats, and ties future-oriented problems to something real today, honestly and without deception.
items.quote: You can also explain how your problem relates, even tangentially, to something real today. (But don't be deceptive about your true motivations.)

items.claim: Treats work in new or contested areas as likely to be rejected for assuming premises the audience hasn't accepted, so he reads rejection as a signal to strengthen the argument rather than abandon the idea.
items.quote: On the first pass, the paper is often rejected because it's saying something a little outside what's normally believed to be true. The reviewers aren't convinced and leave some confused remarks.

items.claim: Wants a result to feel complete, covering the obvious extensions and anticipated critiques, so no 'I wish they had done X' remains, while leaving non-critical directions open.
items.quote: your paper should be at a local optimum; the reader must not be left with the thought "I really wish the authors had done X; that would have been an obvious improvement."
